newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: Southern African group launches productivity drive.
newsitem.headline: Southern African group launches productivity drive.

text.p: Southern African states launched a combined productivity drive on Monday which they said was crucial for foreign investment in the region.

The 12-member Southern African Development Community (SADC) began a 10-day annual conference in the Namibian capital Windhoek to consider ways of pooling resources to boost the region's economic growth.

"Productivity levels and trends will be crucial in attracting foreign investment and enhancing the competitive edge of southern African companies," SADC's executive secretary Kaire Mbuende told a media briefing at the end of the first day.
"We think that we have really not realised the importance of the productivity issue in the region," Mbuende said.

"In the past we could defend our market by imposing high tariffs. But with the signing of the Marrakesh agreement and the establishment of the World Trade Organisation, tariffs are bound to come down and therefore industries are exposed much more than in the past," he added.
He said the region wanted continued preferential access to developing markets to spur regional development.

"As part of an effort to support development in our part of the world we would like to appeal to the WTO and industrialised countries that preferential access on a non-reciprocal basis as existing today between Europe and Southern Africa should be retained," he said.
Mbuende said labour issues, such as poor attitudes to work and pay demands, also affected productivity levels.
"We think it's about time that we address this issue and that we indeed need do develop a national culture of being efficient and productive," he said.
Mbuende stressed the importance of a regional policy to promote productivity and an increased awareness of the issue at enterprise level.
"Productivity should be viewed as a collective responsibility of government, employers and trade unions," he said.
The conference will seek to promote dialogue between all stakeholders when it invites SADC policymakers, business and labour for talks on the issue, Muende said.
SADC comprises Mauritius, Angola, Lesotho, Swaziland, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Namibia, Mozambique, Tanzania, Malawi, South Africa and Botswana.
All these except Botswana, South Africa, Lesotho and Mozambique are also members of COMESA, which also groups Burundi, Comoros, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Kenya, Madagascar, Rwanda, Sudan, Uganda and Zaire.
